questions.stem: The study design names four purposes for students' writing. They are:
options: to describe, to narrate, to inform and to entertain
to persuade, to instruct, to recount and to review
to express, to inform, to persuade and to entertain
to express, to reflect, to explain and to argue
questions.explanation: The study design lists express, reflect, explain and argue, and notes that a piece can have more than one purpose. The other lists are familiar from earlier years but are not the study design's four.

questions.stem: In the study design, writing that explores cause and effect, and the possible consequences of actions, events or ideas, has the purpose:
options: to reflect
to argue
to explain
to express
questions.explanation: Explaining traces causes, effects and consequences. Reflecting explores experiences of personal discovery, and arguing takes a stand to convince others.

questions.stem: A student's piece weighs up what a failed audition revealed to her about her own fears, and how her idea of success has shifted since. Its main purpose is:
options: to argue
to instruct
to report
to reflect
questions.explanation: Exploring a personal discovery and how it changed her understanding is what the study design calls reflecting. She takes no stand for readers to adopt, so the piece is not arguing.

questions.stem: In writing, 'register' refers to:
options: the number of words allowed in a piece set for school assessment
the point of view from which a story is told, such as first person
the level of formality of the language, chosen to suit audience and context
the list of mentor texts a writer has studied before beginning a draft
questions.explanation: Register is how formal or informal language is, from slang to official prose. Point of view concerns who tells a story, not how formal the language is.

questions.stem: Before writing a speech for a school assembly, a student asks: 'Will my audience read this or listen to it?' Which aspect of audience and context is she considering?
options: mode
site
power
cultural understanding
questions.explanation: The study design describes mode as how the audience will receive the writing, by reading or listening. Site is where the writing appears, such as a public or private space.

questions.stem: A Year 11 student writes to the school principal asking for a later start time. Which consideration of audience should most shape her register?
options: the principal is a close friend, so slang will help build rapport quickly
the letter will be heard rather than read, so it needs sound effects
the principal is the same age as her, so casual abbreviations will fit
the principal holds more power, so a respectful, formal register suits
questions.explanation: The study design asks writers to consider who holds power and how formal to be. Writing to a person in authority calls for a respectful, formal register, and nothing suggests the principal is a friend or a peer.

questions.stem: A student adapts her written short story into a podcast episode. Which change best suits the new mode?
options: adding more subheadings to break the story into clearly labelled parts
relying on paragraph breaks and white space to show each change of scene
adding clear spoken signposts and some repetition so listeners can follow
adding footnotes so that listeners can check the story's sources later
questions.explanation: Listeners cannot reread or see the page, so spoken cues and repetition help them keep track. Footnotes, subheadings and paragraph breaks are features of print that a listener never sees.

questions.stem: A student's opinion piece will be pinned to a community noticeboard outside a local supermarket. Which choice best responds to this site?
options: an audio file with background music for shoppers to download later
a bold headline and short, punchy paragraphs readable in passing
long footnoted paragraphs designed for slow, careful study at a desk
a script with stage directions written for a cast of several actors
questions.explanation: The site determines how the audience meets the text, and shoppers will glance at a noticeboard on the move. Long footnoted paragraphs suit a reader at a desk, not a passer-by.

questions.stem: Writing for an international online audience, a student describes a meal as 'a sausage sizzle at Bunnings'. Which consideration from the study design does this choice risk overlooking?
options: formality, since the phrase is too technical for general readers
cultural understanding, since readers may not share the reference
power, since overseas readers hold formal authority over the writer
mode, since online readers will hear the text rather than read it
questions.explanation: The study design asks whether the writer shares the audience's cultural understanding, and an overseas reader may not know this Australian reference. The phrase is casual, not technical, so formality is not the problem.

questions.stem: A student is writing a speech for primary school children about water safety. Which voice suits this audience and purpose best?
options: sarcastic and knowing, to keep the older students in the room amused
formal and abstract, built from long and complex sentences throughout
warm and direct, with simple sentences and one clear message
detached and technical, with a statistic in almost every sentence
questions.explanation: Young listeners need a friendly voice and a message they can easily hold on to. Dense statistics and complex sentences would lose them quickly.

questions.stem: Which opening best suits a feature article about ocean plastic for a teen surfing magazine?
options: ‘Ever paddled out and felt a chip packet wrap around your ankle?’
‘This report outlines measured concentrations of marine plastic in coastal waters.’
‘Dear Minister, I write to express my concern about plastic pollution.’
‘Once upon a time, in a kingdom beneath the waves, there lived a fish.’
questions.explanation: The question addresses surfers directly with an experience they recognise, matching the magazine's audience and informal register. The report-style opening suits a scientific audience, and the letter suits a minister.

questions.stem: A student is choosing a title for a reflective essay about learning to swim as an adult. Which title best signals both its subject and its reflective purpose?
options: Learning to Float at Forty
Ten Quick Tips for Adult Swimmers
Why Councils Must Fund More Pools
Pool Opening Hours for Summer Announced
questions.explanation: The first title hints at a personal experience and what it meant to the writer. The tips title signals instructions, the council title signals an argument, and the last signals a news report.

questions.stem: Which sentence shows, rather than tells, that a character is nervous?
options: Everyone in the room could tell that she was feeling very anxious.
She felt nervous, as she always seemed to in situations like these.
Her pen clicked, clicked, clicked against the desk as the results were read.
She was extremely nervous about hearing the results being read out.
questions.explanation: The repeated clicking pen lets readers infer her nerves from an action. The other sentences state the feeling outright, which is telling.

questions.stem: ‘The market smelt of diesel and frying onions, and a radio crackled somewhere behind the fish stall.’ The writer's main technique is:
options: an extended metaphor comparing the market to a ship at sea
sensory imagery that immerses the reader in the setting
rhetorical questioning that involves the reader directly
a flashback revealing the narrator's childhood past
questions.explanation: Smell and sound details place the reader inside the market. There is no question, no shift in time and no comparison, so the other techniques are absent.

questions.stem: ‘Grief is a house with no doors.’ This sentence is an example of:
options: an oxymoron
a rhetorical question
a metaphor
a simile
questions.explanation: Grief is described as being a house, without 'like' or 'as', so it is a metaphor. A simile would say grief is like a house.

questions.stem: A student revises 'the old dog walked across the yard' to 'the old dog shuffled across the yard'. The revision is effective mainly because:
options: the change adds alliteration, which makes any sentence more effective
longer words always make a piece of writing sound more sophisticated
the precise verb conveys age and stiffness without adding adjectives
the new verb makes the sentence noticeably more formal in its register
questions.explanation: 'Shuffled' carries the dog's age and slowness within a single word. The change does not create alliteration, and length alone never makes writing better.

questions.stem: ‘The anemometer spun; gusts hit 90 km/h by noon.’ This sentence mainly uses:
options: abstract nouns to express the writer's feelings
figurative language to entertain a young audience
technical vocabulary and data to inform
colloquial language to build intimacy with the reader
questions.explanation: 'Anemometer' is a technical term and the wind speed is precise data, which suits writing to inform or explain. Nothing in the sentence is colloquial or figurative.

questions.stem: Expanding 'a house' to 'a sagging weatherboard house at the end of a dirt road' mainly:
options: changes the sentence from the active to the passive voice
turns the phrase into a rhetorical question for the reader
builds a precise picture through an expanded noun group
adds a subordinate clause that shows cause and effect
questions.explanation: Adjectives and a prepositional phrase are added around the noun 'house', creating an expanded noun group. There is no clause with its own verb, so no cause and effect is shown.

questions.stem: A student's paragraph uses only long compound sentences. Adding one short sentence at the key moment would most likely:
options: slow the pace of the paragraph down by adding more descriptive detail
shift the point of view of the whole paragraph into the third person
create emphasis by breaking the rhythm the paragraph has set up
turn the paragraph into a formal argument with a stated contention
questions.explanation: A short sentence among long ones stands out and lands with force. A short sentence adds less detail, not more, so it does not slow the pace that way.

questions.stem: A memoir piece opens: 'The day the factory closed, Dad came home at noon and mowed the lawn.' It then moves back through his working life before returning to that afternoon. This structure is best described as:
options: a numbered list, with each memory presented as a separate point
circular, beginning and ending at the same moment to frame the memories
strictly chronological, moving steadily from the earliest event to the latest
in medias res, with no return to the scene the piece opens with
questions.explanation: The piece starts and ends on the same afternoon, which frames the memories between. It does open mid-story, but it clearly returns to that scene, so 'no return' is wrong.

questions.stem: A reflective piece reads: 'You learn to read the sky. You learn which clouds mean you bring the sheep in.' The main effect of the second person here is to:
options: create distance by describing the events from far outside them
reveal the private thoughts of many different characters at once
draw readers into the experience as if it were their own
signal an objective, scientific explanation of weather patterns
questions.explanation: The generalised 'you' places the reader inside the learning, which creates closeness. It does the opposite of creating distance.

questions.stem: ‘Slowly, softly, the snow settled on the silent street.’ The main sound device in this sentence is:
options: alliteration, with repeated s sounds creating a hush
onomatopoeia, imitating the sound of the falling snow
end rhyme, linking the final words of two lines
a rhetorical question, inviting the reader to reply
questions.explanation: Most words begin with s, and the soft sound suits the quiet scene. None of the words imitates a sound, so it is not onomatopoeia.

questions.stem: Which revision would most improve the cohesion of a feature article whose paragraphs jump between topics?
options: shortening every paragraph in the article to a single sentence each
adding linking sentences and grouping related ideas into ordered sections
replacing common words throughout with more technical vocabulary
adding exclamation marks at the end of paragraphs to keep readers alert
questions.explanation: The study design describes cohesive writing as interconnected ideas presented in a clear and organised way, which linking and grouping achieve. Technical vocabulary changes the register, not how the ideas connect.

questions.stem: ‘They call it a “minor” spill. Tell that to the pelicans.’ The writer's language mainly works by:
options: using neutral data and measurements to explain the spill's causes
using a simile to compare the oil spill directly to the pelicans
using a formal register to praise the official response to the spill
using sarcasm and a vivid image to challenge an official description
questions.explanation: The quotation marks around 'minor' signal scorn, and the pelicans make the harm concrete. There is no comparison using 'like' or 'as', so it is not a simile.

questions.stem: ‘We will not be the generation that looked away.’ A writer most likely uses this sentence to:
options: rally the audience through a shared identity and a sense of responsibility
explain the scientific causes of a problem in calm, neutral terms
reflect privately on a single personal memory from early childhood
describe a physical setting in vivid and carefully chosen sensory detail
questions.explanation: 'We' and 'generation' bind the audience together, and 'looked away' shames inaction, which shows the power of language to achieve a writer's aims. Nothing in the sentence is neutral or scientific.

questions.stem: Colloquial language is:
options: the formal language used in official documents and legal contracts
informal, everyday language used in conversation, including slang
the specialised terms used within a particular profession or field
language that imitates the sounds of the things it describes
questions.explanation: Colloquial language is the language of casual speech, such as 'arvo' or 'no worries'. Specialised professional terms are jargon, which is a different thing.

questions.stem: In a short story, a teenage character texts: 'omg cant even rn'. This non-standard language is appropriate because it:
options: follows the spelling conventions of Standard Australian English
makes the piece more suitable for a formal academic audience
replaces the need for any other characterisation in the story
creates an authentic voice for the character in that context
questions.explanation: The study design allows non-standard conventions where they suit audience, purpose and context, and this text message sounds like a real teenager. It deliberately breaks standard spelling and punctuation rather than following them.

questions.stem: A writer has an elderly character say: 'We was flat out like a lizard drinking.' Using this dialect and idiom mainly:
options: makes the dialogue suitable for inclusion in an academic report
replaces the need for any description of the story's setting
builds a distinct voice grounded in a particular place and community
signals that the character comes from a formal, highly educated background
questions.explanation: Non-standard grammar and an Australian idiom meaning very busy give the character an authentic, local voice. They work against an impression of formality.

questions.stem: In an informative piece for a council newsletter, which sentence follows the conventions of Standard Australian English?
options: Resident's bins will be collected on Tuesdays' from next month.
Residents' bins will be collected on Tuesday's from next month.
Residents' bins will be collected on Tuesdays from next month.
Residents bins will be collected on Tuesday's from next month.
questions.explanation: 'Residents'' is a plural possessive and 'Tuesdays' is a simple plural that needs no apostrophe. Adding an apostrophe to a plain plural, as in 'Tuesday's', is a common error.

questions.stem: A mentor text is:
options: a text read and re-read as a model of effective writing
a text a teacher writes to correct a student's draft
a set text studied in order to write an analytical essay
a guide that sets out the rules of grammar and spelling
questions.explanation: The study design defines mentor texts as texts to be read and re-read as models of effective and cohesive writing. They are studied for how they are written, not as set texts for analysis.

questions.stem: Which is a strategy for generating ideas before drafting?
options: checking that the word count of the final draft is within the limit
formatting the published piece with a heading and an attractive font
freewriting for ten minutes in response to an image from a mentor text
proofreading a finished piece carefully for spelling and grammar errors
questions.explanation: Freewriting is a pre-writing strategy that gets ideas flowing before any draft exists. Proofreading and formatting belong to the last stages of writing.

questions.stem: Which order best reflects the writing processes described in the study design?
options: draft, publish, brainstorm, edit, revise
edit, brainstorm, publish, draft, revise
publish, draft, revise, brainstorm, edit
brainstorm, draft, revise, edit, publish
questions.explanation: Writing moves from pre-writing such as brainstorming, through drafting, revising, refining and editing, to publishing. Writers often loop back, but publishing comes last.

questions.stem: A student moves her climax earlier and cuts a whole subplot from her draft. This stage of writing is best called:
options: revising, which reshapes the content and structure
editing, which corrects the spelling and punctuation
publishing, which presents the final finished copy
brainstorming, which gathers the first rough ideas
questions.explanation: Revising involves large changes to content and structure, like moving a climax. Editing works at the level of sentences, spelling and punctuation.

questions.stem: A peer says the opening of a student's story 'drags'. What is the most effective response to this feedback?
options: delete the whole piece and start again on a completely different idea
ignore the comment, since only feedback from a teacher should count
add more description to the opening so that readers slow down further
reread the opening for pace and test a tighter version against the original
questions.explanation: Feedback is most useful when the writer tests it against the draft and decides what works. Adding description would make a slow opening slower still.

questions.stem: Two peers give a writer conflicting feedback: one wants more dialogue, the other less. What should the writer do?
options: ignore both comments, since feedback only slows the writing process down
weigh each suggestion against her purpose and audience, then decide
follow whichever peer is the stronger writer, without rereading the draft
follow whichever comment she received first and set the other one aside
questions.explanation: The writer is responsible for her choices, and purpose and audience are the test of whether more dialogue helps. Deferring to a person rather than to the needs of the piece skips that judgement.

questions.stem: Why does the study design value collaboration and discussion during writing?
options: sharing drafts tests whether choices work for real readers and sparks new ideas
discussion lets a group write one shared piece that every student then submits
talking about writing replaces the need for students to revise their own work
classmates are always the intended audience of every piece that students write
questions.explanation: Discussion and feedback show how a draft lands with readers and help writers generate and refine ideas. Each student still drafts and revises their own individual writing.

questions.stem: While reading a mentor text, a student notices that the writer opens each section with a single remembered smell. How can she best use this observation?
options: experiment with a similar structural device in her own piece on another subject
copy the mentor text's opening sentences into her own piece word for word
set structure aside and focus only on the mentor text's spelling and punctuation
summarise the mentor text's events so she can include them in her commentary
questions.explanation: Mentor texts are models: students borrow techniques and adapt them to their own ideas. Copying sentences word for word would be plagiarism, not learning from a model.

questions.stem: Two mentor texts explore 'home': one is a poem about a refugee's lost village, the other a comic essay about sharing a bedroom. This mainly shows that:
options: only serious, formal forms are suited to exploring an idea as large as home
comic writing cannot meaningfully address an idea such as belonging or home
both of the mentor texts must have been written by the same author
one idea can be explored through many different forms, tones and perspectives
questions.explanation: The study design notes the range of ideas presented in various ways in mentor texts, and these two treat one idea very differently. The comic essay shows that humour can explore home too.

questions.stem: In a description of her writing processes, which sentence best explains an authorial choice?
options: I think the story turned out quite well and my friends all enjoyed it.
I left the narrator unnamed so readers could imagine themselves in her place.
I wrote the story over two weekends, mostly at the desk in my bedroom.
My story is about a girl and her dog on a windy day at the beach.
questions.explanation: An effective description names a deliberate choice and the effect it was meant to have on readers. Where and when the story was written, or what it is about, explains no choice.

questions.stem: A student turns her persuasive essay into a speech and adds lines such as 'Picture this…' and 'So I ask you…'. These changes mainly:
options: suit the spoken mode by engaging a listening audience directly
make the text better suited to silent, private reading at home
shift the purpose of the piece from arguing to explaining causes
add technical vocabulary to satisfy an expert, specialist audience
questions.explanation: Direct address and invitations to imagine hold listeners' attention in a spoken mode. They do nothing to change the purpose, which is still to argue.

questions.stem: A short story ends with a character refusing to sign a petition, and the narrator observing: 'Silence, too, is a choice.' This line adds which purpose to the story's expressive one?
options: explaining, by setting out the scientific causes of the issue
instructing, by giving readers the steps for signing petitions
describing, by building the setting through sensory detail
arguing, by implying a view the reader is invited to share
questions.explanation: The narrator's comment takes a stand that staying silent is a moral choice, so the story also argues. The line traces no causes, so it is not explaining.
